dx: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) with hypocalcemic tetany and truncus arteriosus
case: A 4-day-old boy in the neonatal intensive care unit develops carpopedal spasm and brief generalized jerking movements. A murmur was heard at birth, and echocardiography showed truncus arteriosus. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 156/min, respirations are 52/min, and blood pressure is 68/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows low-set ears, a short philtrum, micrognathia, and a cleft of the soft palate. Serum total calcium concentration is 6.1 mg/dL (N = 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL). A chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow. Diagnosis: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome) with hypocalcemic tetany and truncus arteriosus.

questions.stem: Additional serum studies are obtained. Which of the following sets of findings best explains his tetany?
options: High parathyroid hormone and low phosphorus
Low parathyroid hormone and high phosphorus
High parathyroid hormone and high phosphorus
Low parathyroid hormone and low phosphorus
approach: Link the missing thymus to failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
Those pouches also form the parathyroid glands, so parathyroid hormone (PTH) is low.
Without PTH, calcium falls and the kidney keeps phosphate, so phosphorus rises.
questions.why: In 22q11.2 deletion syndrome the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches develop poorly. The third pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroids, and the fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroids. Parathyroid hypoplasia gives primary hypoparathyroidism. Low PTH lowers bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and calcitriol synthesis, so calcium falls. PTH also normally makes the kidney excrete phosphate, so its absence raises serum phosphorus. The same pouch failure explains the absent thymic shadow, and abnormal neural crest migration explains the conotruncal heart defect.
whyNot: High PTH with low phosphorus is secondary hyperparathyroidism, as in vitamin D deficiency, where the parathyroids are intact and respond to low calcium.
Correct.
High PTH with high phosphorus fits chronic kidney disease or PTH resistance (pseudohypoparathyroidism), where the glands are present but the response fails.
Low PTH removes the phosphaturic effect of the hormone, so phosphorus rises rather than falls.

questions.stem: The organ that is missing on his chest x-ray normally develops from the same pharyngeal pouch as which of the following structures?
options: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid
approach: Identify the missing organ as the thymus.
Recall that the thymus comes from the endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch.
The other derivative of the third pouch is the pair of inferior parathyroid glands.
questions.why: The thymic epithelium arises from the ventral part of the third pharyngeal pouch, and the dorsal part of the same pouch forms the inferior parathyroids. Neural crest cells form the thymic capsule and septa. As the thymus descends into the anterior mediastinum, it pulls the third pouch parathyroids down with it. That is why the third pouch glands end up below the fourth pouch glands.
whyNot: The superior parathyroid glands come from the fourth pharyngeal pouch. They do not migrate with the thymus, so they end up higher.
Parafollicular C cells come from the ultimobranchial body of the fourth pouch region, with neural crest contribution.
The palatine tonsil epithelium comes from the second pharyngeal pouch.
Correct.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry shows a markedly low CD3+ T cell count with normal B cell and natural killer cell counts. His bone marrow lymphoid progenitors are normal. Which of the following best explains the low T cell count?
options: Absent thymic epithelium for precursor maturation
Failure of marrow stem cells to form lymphoid progenitors
Defective recombination of T cell receptor gene segments
Loss of interleukin-7 receptor signaling in thymocytes
approach: Note that the marrow makes normal lymphoid progenitors.
T cell precursors must leave the marrow and mature inside a thymic epithelial framework.
A hypoplastic thymus gives the precursors nowhere to mature, so T cells are low while B and NK cells are normal.
questions.why: The thymus begins as an endodermal epithelial framework. During fetal life, T cell precursors from the bone marrow (and earlier from fetal liver) colonize it. The epithelial reticular cells then organize an outer cortex packed with developing thymocytes and an inner medulla with Hassall corpuscles. In DiGeorge syndrome this epithelial framework is small or absent. Normal precursors arrive but cannot mature, so T cells are low while B and NK cells are normal.
whyNot: Correct.
A stem cell defect in lymphoid progenitor formation, as in reticular dysgenesis, would also remove B and NK cells.
Failed T cell receptor gene recombination, as in RAG deficiency, would also block B cell development because B cells use the same recombinase.
Loss of interleukin-7 receptor signaling causes a lymphocyte-intrinsic form of SCID with a normal thymic epithelium. It does not explain the absent thymus in this infant.

questions.stem: Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the underlying genetic abnormality?
options: PCR sizing of a trinucleotide repeat
Methylation analysis of an imprinted region
approach: Recognize the typical features of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome: conotruncal defect, facial changes, cleft palate, thymic hypoplasia, and hypocalcemia.
Recall that the deletion is usually about 3 Mb, too small to see on a routine karyotype.
Choose a test that detects small copy number losses, such as chromosomal microarray or FISH.
questions.why: Most patients have a deletion of about 3 Mb on the long arm of chromosome 22. Loss of one copy of TBX1 in the deleted segment is thought to drive the pharyngeal arch, cardiac outflow, and palate defects. A standard karyotype cannot see deletions this small, so it is usually normal. Chromosomal microarray detects the copy number loss, and FISH with a 22q11.2 probe can also confirm it.
whyNot: A G-banded karyotype resolves changes of about 5 Mb or more, so the typical 22q11.2 microdeletion is missed.
Trinucleotide repeat sizing diagnoses expansion disorders such as fragile X syndrome or Huntington disease.
Correct.
Methylation analysis diagnoses imprinting disorders such as Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome.

dx: Severe combined immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase deficiency
case: A 7-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of cough and fast breathing for 4 days. She has had watery diarrhea and poor weight gain since age 3 months and three courses of treatment for oral thrush. Her parents are first cousins. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 152/min, respirations are 58/min, and blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg. Weight is below the 3rd percentile. Physical examination shows white plaques on the buccal mucosa, no palpable lymph nodes, and no visible tonsils. Absolute lymphocyte count is 350/mm3 (N = 4,000 to 13,500/mm3). A chest x-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates and no thymic shadow. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows Pneumocystis jirovecii. Erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity is absent. Diagnosis: severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) from adenosine deaminase deficiency.

questions.stem: A deoxynucleotide accumulates in her lymphocytes and leads to their death. This metabolite inhibits which of the following enzymes?
approach: Adenosine deaminase normally converts adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine.
Without it, deoxyadenosine is phosphorylated and dATP builds up, especially in lymphocytes.
dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, so the cell cannot make deoxynucleotides for DNA synthesis.
questions.why: Adenosine deaminase is part of purine salvage. When it is missing, deoxyadenosine accumulates and lymphocytes phosphorylate it to dATP. High dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, the enzyme that makes all four deoxyribonucleotides. Dividing lymphocytes can no longer synthesize DNA and die. T, B, and NK cells are all lost, and inheritance is autosomal recessive, which fits her consanguineous parents.
whyNot: Thymidylate synthase makes dTMP from dUMP. It is the target of 5-fluorouracil, not of dATP.
Dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate. It is the target of methotrexate and trimethoprim.
Correct.
Glutamine PRPP amidotransferase is the committed step of de novo purine synthesis. It is feedback-inhibited by purine nucleotides, but that does not explain lymphocyte death in this disease.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry of her peripheral blood is most likely to show which of the following patterns?
options: Absent T cells, absent B cells, absent NK cells
Absent T cells, normal B cells, absent NK cells
Absent T cells, absent B cells, normal NK cells
Normal T cells, absent B cells, normal NK cells
approach: Recall that toxic dATP harms every developing lymphocyte line.
So ADA deficiency removes T, B, and NK cells together.
Compare the other SCID genotypes, which spare one line.
questions.why: SCID genotypes are sorted by which lymphocytes remain. ADA deficiency poisons all lymphocyte lines, so T, B, and NK cells are all absent. X-linked SCID from a common gamma chain (IL2RG) mutation removes T and NK cells but leaves nonfunctional B cells. RAG deficiency removes T and B cells but spares NK cells, which do not rearrange receptor genes. All forms have very low T cell receptor excision circles on newborn screening because few T cells leave the thymus.
whyNot: Correct.
Absent T and NK cells with B cells present is the pattern of X-linked SCID from a common gamma chain mutation.
Absent T and B cells with NK cells present is the pattern of RAG1 or RAG2 deficiency.
Absent B cells with normal T and NK cells is the pattern of X-linked agammaglobulinemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following exposures would pose the greatest risk to this patient before her immune system is reconstituted?
approach: Recognize that she has no functional T or B cells.
A live vaccine organism can replicate unchecked and cause disseminated disease.
Inactivated vaccines, irradiated blood, and immune globulin carry no replicating agent or viable donor lymphocytes.
questions.why: Infants with SCID cannot control even weakened organisms. Live vaccines such as rotavirus, BCG, and oral polio can cause severe or fatal vaccine-strain infection, so they are withheld. Blood products must be irradiated (and CMV-safe) because viable donor T cells in nonirradiated blood can engraft and attack the host as transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. Immune globulin replacement and Pneumocystis prophylaxis are standard until stem cell transplantation or other definitive treatment.
whyNot: An inactivated vaccine cannot replicate. It is safe, though she may not mount an antibody response to it.
Irradiation inactivates donor lymphocytes, so this is the safe way to transfuse a patient with SCID.
Immune globulin is part of her treatment and replaces the antibodies she cannot make.
Correct.

questions.stem: At autopsy of a similar infant, the thymus is tiny, with scattered epithelial cells, almost no thymocytes, no Hassall corpuscles, and no distinction between cortex and medulla. In a normal infant thymus, which of the following features identifies the cortex?
approach: Recall the layout of a thymic lobule: dark outer cortex and pale inner medulla.
The cortex is dark because it is packed with immature thymocytes on an epithelial reticular network.
The medulla holds fewer, more mature T cells and Hassall corpuscles.
questions.why: Each thymic lobule has a darkly staining cortex and a paler medulla. The cortex is crowded with immature, dividing thymocytes held in a mesh of epithelial reticular cells. Its capillaries form the blood thymus barrier, which limits blood-borne antigen while T cells develop. The medulla contains fewer, more mature T cells and the concentric keratinized Hassall corpuscles. In SCID the thymus never fills with thymocytes, so this cortex and medulla pattern does not form.
whyNot: Hassall corpuscles are whorls of keratinized epithelial reticular cells found in the medulla.
Correct.
Loosely packed mature T cells give the medulla its pale staining.
Germinal centers are B cell structures in lymph node and splenic follicles. The normal thymus does not contain them.

case: A 14-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever and cough. Since age 8 months he has had three episodes of otitis media and one of pneumonia. His mother's brother died of infection in early childhood. Temperature is 39.0 °C (102.2 °F), pulse is 142/min, respirations are 44/min, and blood pressure is 90/56 mm Hg. He has barely visible tonsils and no palpable cervical lymph nodes. A chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae. Serum IgG is 80 mg/dL (N = 350 to 1,200 mg/dL), IgA is undetectable (N = 15 to 100 mg/dL), and IgM is 10 mg/dL (N = 40 to 150 mg/dL). CD19+ B cells are less than 1% of lymphocytes (N = 13% to 35%). T and NK cell counts are normal. Diagnosis: X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the defect in this patient's B cell development?
options: Class switch failure from absent CD40 ligand
Plasma cell differentiation failure in mature B cells
Heavy chain gene segment recombination failure
Pre-B cell arrest from defective kinase signaling
approach: Note absent circulating B cells with normal T cells and very low levels of every immunoglobulin class.
X-linked inheritance through the maternal side points to the BTK gene.
Bruton tyrosine kinase carries the pre-B cell receptor signal, so B cells stop at the pre-B stage.
questions.why: Bruton tyrosine kinase transmits signals from the pre-B cell receptor that tell the cell to proliferate and continue maturing. When BTK is mutated, B cell development stops at the pre-B stage in the bone marrow. Few mature B cells reach the blood, so follicles, tonsils, and all immunoglobulin classes are markedly reduced. Infections begin after about 6 months, when maternal IgG that crossed the placenta has been used up.
whyNot: Absent CD40 ligand causes X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome. B cell numbers are normal and IgM is normal or high.
Failed plasma cell differentiation with normal B cell numbers describes common variable immunodeficiency.
Failed gene segment recombination from RAG deficiency would also prevent T cell development and cause SCID. This boy's T cells are normal.
Correct.

questions.stem: Another infant has absent T cells and B cells but normal natural killer cells. The defect lies in the first step of antigen receptor gene rearrangement, a step that this patient's pre-B cells complete normally. Which of the following activities is most likely defective in that infant?
options: Addition of nontemplated nucleotides at junctions
Deamination of cytidine in switch regions
Signaling through the common gamma chain
approach: Absent T and B cells with spared NK cells means a defect shared only by cells that rearrange receptor genes.
V(D)J recombination begins when RAG1 and RAG2 cut DNA at recombination signal sequences.
Without these cuts no T cell receptor or immunoglobulin can form, so both lines fail.
questions.why: T and B cells both build their antigen receptors by V(D)J recombination. RAG1 and RAG2 make double-strand breaks at recombination signal sequences next to each gene segment, and DNA repair enzymes join the segments. TdT then adds random nucleotides at the joints, which increases junctional diversity. RAG deficiency blocks receptor formation, so T and B cells are absent, while NK cells, which do not rearrange receptor genes, remain. In XLA the RAG step is intact and the block comes later.
whyNot: TdT adds nontemplated nucleotides. Losing it reduces junctional diversity, but receptors still form, so it does not cause SCID.
Correct.
Activation-induced cytidine deaminase works in class switching and somatic hypermutation. Its loss gives an autosomal hyper-IgM syndrome with normal B cell numbers.
Loss of common gamma chain signaling causes X-linked SCID with absent T and NK cells and present B cells, which does not match.

questions.stem: In addition to infections with encapsulated bacteria, this patient is at particular risk for which of the following?
approach: Identify the defective arm: antibody production (B cells).
Antibody defects allow encapsulated bacteria, Giardia, and enteroviruses, which are controlled mainly by neutralizing antibody.
Match each distractor to its own defective arm.
questions.why: The infection pattern points to the defective arm of immunity. B cell defects give infections with encapsulated bacteria (which need antibody for opsonization), Giardia, and enteroviruses (which are neutralized by antibody). Boys with XLA can develop chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis, and live oral polio vaccine can cause vaccine-associated paralysis. The first test for a suspected B cell defect is serum immunoglobulin levels, followed by flow cytometry for B cells.
whyNot: Disseminated mycobacterial infection points to a defect in the IL-12 and interferon-gamma pathway or a T cell defect.
Recurrent Neisseria bacteremia points to a terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency. The screening test is CH50.
Correct.
Invasive aspergillosis points to a phagocyte defect such as chronic granulomatous disease or severe neutropenia.

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy from this patient would most likely show depletion of which of the following regions?
approach: Match each lymph node zone to its main cell type.
B cells live in the cortical follicles and form germinal centers there.
With almost no mature B cells, follicles and germinal centers are absent or tiny.
questions.why: Lymph node B cells gather in cortical follicles, which form germinal centers after antigen exposure. T cells occupy the paracortex. In XLA, B cells are nearly absent, so nodes and tonsils are small and lack follicles and germinal centers. The paracortex is preserved. The opposite pattern occurs in DiGeorge syndrome, where the paracortex is depleted and follicles are intact.
whyNot: Correct.
The paracortex is the T cell zone. It is depleted in T cell defects such as DiGeorge syndrome.
Medullary sinuses carry lymph past macrophages. They do not depend on B cells and are not depleted here.
The subcapsular sinus receives afferent lymph and is lined by macrophages. It is not a B cell zone.

dx: Common variable immunodeficiency with chronic giardiasis
case: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea, bloating, and a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss over 2 months. She has had four episodes of sinusitis and two episodes of pneumonia during the past 3 years. She was healthy as a child. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is mildly distended and nontender. Stool antigen testing is positive for Giardia duodenalis. Serum IgG is 210 mg/dL (N = 700 to 1,600 mg/dL), IgA is 15 mg/dL (N = 70 to 400 mg/dL), and IgM is 25 mg/dL (N = 40 to 230 mg/dL). She has no antibody response to tetanus or pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccines. Diagnosis: common variable immunodeficiency with chronic giardiasis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the defect underlying her immunodeficiency?
options: Normal B cells that fail to become plasma cells
Absent B cells from arrest at the pre-B cell stage
Absent T cells from failed thymic development
Low NK cells from a common gamma chain defect
approach: Note adult onset, low IgG and IgA, and absent vaccine responses.
This is common variable immunodeficiency, in which B cells are present but do not mature into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
So the B cell count is usually normal, which separates it from XLA.
questions.why: In common variable immunodeficiency, most patients have normal numbers of circulating B cells. The defect is in their differentiation into plasma cells, so IgG and IgA (and often IgM) are low and vaccine responses fail. It often begins in the second to fourth decade. Patients get sinopulmonary infections and Giardia, and they have higher rates of autoimmune disease (such as autoimmune cytopenias), granulomatous disease, and B cell lymphoma.
whyNot: Correct.
Absent B cells from a pre-B cell block is X-linked agammaglobulinemia, which presents in infant boys.
Absent T cells from thymic failure is DiGeorge syndrome, which would bring viral and fungal infections and normal B cell function.
Common gamma chain defects cause X-linked SCID in infancy, with absent T and NK cells.

questions.stem: Monthly intravenous immune globulin is started. The infused IgG promotes phagocytosis of bacteria by binding receptors on neutrophils and macrophages. Which portion of the IgG molecule binds these receptors?
options: Constant domain of the light chains
Fc region of the heavy chains
approach: Separate the two jobs of an antibody: the Fab binds antigen and the Fc carries out effector functions.
Phagocytes carry Fc gamma receptors.
So opsonization depends on the Fc region formed by the heavy chain constant domains.
questions.why: IgG has two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains. The two Fab arms each contain hypervariable regions from both chains that form the antigen-binding site. The Fc region is made only of heavy chain constant domains. It sets the isotype's functions, including binding Fc receptors on phagocytes (opsonization) and binding C1q to start the classical complement pathway. Replacement IgG coats bacteria through its Fab and links them to phagocytes through its Fc.
whyNot: Hypervariable regions in the Fab bind the antigen itself. They determine specificity, not effector function.
Light chains help form the Fab. They do not take part in Fc receptor binding.
Correct.
The J chain joins IgA dimers and IgM pentamers. IgG is a monomer without a J chain.

questions.stem: Secretory IgA helps clear Giardia from the small intestine. Which of the following cells normally take up luminal antigen to start the intestinal IgA response?
approach: The IgA response begins in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, mainly the Peyer patches of the ileum.
Specialized epithelial cells over these patches transport antigen from the lumen to the immune cells beneath.
Those cells are M (microfold) cells.
questions.why: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue includes the tonsils and the Peyer patches of the ileum. M cells in the epithelium over Peyer patches take up luminal antigens and pass them to dendritic cells and lymphocytes in the dome below. B cells there switch to IgA under T cell and cytokine signals such as TGF-beta. They become plasma cells that home to the lamina propria and secrete IgA that is carried across the epithelium into the lumen.
whyNot: Paneth cells secrete defensins and lysozyme. They do not transport antigen to lymphoid tissue.
Correct.
Goblet cells secrete mucus, which forms a barrier but does not start the IgA response.
Enteroendocrine cells secrete hormones such as CCK and secretin. They do not sample antigen.

questions.stem: An enlarged cervical lymph node is removed to exclude lymphoma. In a normal lymph node, the antibody-secreting cells that she fails to produce in adequate numbers are located mainly in which of the following regions?
approach: Identify the missing cells as plasma cells.
Recall the lymph node layout from capsule inward: subcapsular sinus, cortex with follicles, paracortex, then medulla.
Plasma cells collect in the medullary cords, near the medullary sinuses that lead to efferent lymph.
questions.why: Lymph enters a node through afferent vessels into the subcapsular sinus. The outer cortex holds B cell follicles, and primary follicles become secondary follicles with germinal centers after antigen exposure. The paracortex holds T cells and high endothelial venules. The medulla has medullary cords rich in plasma cells and macrophages, separated by medullary sinuses that drain to the efferent lymphatic. Antibody made in the cords enters the efferent lymph and reaches the blood.
whyNot: The paracortex is the T cell zone, where naive T cells enter through high endothelial venules.
The subcapsular sinus receives afferent lymph and is lined by macrophages.
Primary follicles hold resting naive B cells that have not yet met antigen.
Correct.

dx: Selective IgA deficiency with anaphylactic transfusion reaction
case: A 26-year-old woman receives a transfusion of packed red blood cells after blood loss during an emergency appendectomy. Within 5 minutes of starting the transfusion, she develops flushing, diffuse hives, wheezing, and light-headedness. She has had frequent sinus infections since childhood and has never received blood products. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows diffuse urticaria and expiratory wheezes. The transfusion is stopped and she is treated. Serum IgA is undetectable (N = 70 to 400 mg/dL), and IgG and IgM are normal. Anti-IgA antibodies are present. Diagnosis: selective IgA deficiency with an anaphylactic transfusion reaction.

questions.stem: Two years later, she develops chronic diarrhea, bloating, and iron deficiency anemia, and celiac disease is suspected. Which of the following serologic tests is most appropriate?
approach: Recall that selective IgA deficiency is associated with celiac disease.
Standard celiac screening measures IgA autoantibodies, which she cannot make.
So IgA-based tests are falsely negative, and an IgG-based test is needed.
questions.why: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency, and most patients have no symptoms. Some have sinopulmonary or Giardia infections, and celiac and other autoimmune diseases are more common. Because the usual celiac screening tests detect IgA antibodies, they are falsely negative in these patients. IgG-based tests, such as IgG antibody to tissue transglutaminase or to deamidated gliadin peptides, are used instead.
whyNot: IgA tissue transglutaminase is the usual screening test, but she cannot make IgA, so the result would be falsely negative.
Correct.
IgA endomysial antibody is specific for celiac disease, but it is also IgA-based and would be falsely negative.
IgE to wheat detects IgE-mediated wheat allergy, a type I reaction. Celiac disease is a T cell-mediated response to gluten.

questions.stem: Despite the absence of IgA, her mucosal infections have been mild. Which of the following immunoglobulins is most likely carried into her mucosal secretions by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor in increased amounts to compensate?
approach: Ask how an antibody reaches mucosal secretions: the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor carries it across the epithelium.
This receptor binds antibodies that contain a J chain.
Besides dimeric IgA, the only J chain antibody is pentameric IgM.
questions.why: Secretory IgA is a dimer joined by a J chain. The polymeric immunoglobulin receptor on epithelial cells binds the J chain antibody and carries it across into the lumen, and part of the receptor stays on as secretory component. Pentameric IgM also has a J chain, so it uses the same transport route. In IgA deficiency, secretory IgM often increases and partly takes over the mucosal role. IgM is also the first isotype made in a primary response and the strongest activator of complement.
whyNot: Correct.
IgD is a monomer that serves mainly as a receptor on naive B cells. It is not transported into secretions.
IgE is a monomer bound to mast cells and basophils. It is not carried into secretions by the polymeric receptor.
IgG is a monomer without a J chain, so the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor does not carry it. It crosses the placenta through the neonatal Fc receptor instead.

questions.stem: Her reaction had the clinical features of type I hypersensitivity. In type I hypersensitivity, the immediate reaction is often followed hours later by a second wave of swelling and airway narrowing without further exposure. Which of the following best explains this late-phase reaction?
options: Immune complex deposition in small vessels
Th1 cell activation of tissue macrophages
approach: Separate the two phases: the immediate phase comes from mediators released within minutes when mast cells degranulate.
Mast cells also make lipid mediators and cytokines that recruit eosinophils and other leukocytes.
These recruited cells and newly made leukotrienes cause the late phase hours later.
questions.why: In type I hypersensitivity, a first exposure drives Th2 cells and IL-4 to switch B cells to IgE, which binds FcepsilonRI on mast cells. On re-exposure, antigen cross-links this IgE, and mast cells release stored histamine and tryptase within minutes. They also synthesize leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and cytokines that recruit eosinophils, neutrophils, and Th2 cells. About 2 to 24 hours later, these cells and leukotrienes such as LTC4 and LTD4 produce the late phase, with tissue swelling and sustained bronchoconstriction.
whyNot: Immune complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity, as in serum sickness, which appears 1 to 2 weeks after exposure.
Th1 activation of macrophages is type IV hypersensitivity, which peaks 48 to 72 hours after exposure.
Preformed histamine is released in the first minutes and is short-lived, so it explains the immediate phase.
Correct.

questions.stem: In a healthy person, most of the secretory IgA in respiratory and intestinal secretions is produced by plasma cells located in which of the following sites?
approach: Secretory IgA must cross the mucosal epithelium, so it is made close to that epithelium.
IgA plasma cells arise in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue and home back to the mucosa.
They settle in the lamina propria just beneath the epithelium.
questions.why: B cells activated in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, such as tonsils and Peyer patches, switch to IgA and leave through the lymph. They return to mucosal surfaces throughout the body and settle in the lamina propria as plasma cells. There they secrete dimeric IgA, which the overlying epithelium carries into the lumen. This shared mucosal homing is why a response started in the gut can protect other mucosal surfaces.
whyNot: Medullary cord plasma cells release antibody into efferent lymph and then the blood, not directly into mucosal secretions.
Splenic red pulp plasma cells add antibody to the blood. They do not supply mucosal secretions.
Correct.
Bone marrow plasma cells make most serum IgG and the monomeric serum IgA, not the dimeric secretory IgA.

dx: X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency) with Pneumocystis pneumonia
case: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever, dry cough, and increasing difficulty breathing for 5 days. Since age 9 months he has had recurrent otitis media, two episodes of pneumonia, and Cryptosporidium diarrhea. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse is 148/min, respirations are 50/min, and blood pressure is 92/56 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Diffuse fine crackles are heard. A chest x-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Silver stain of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid shows cysts of Pneumocystis jirovecii. Serum IgM is 320 mg/dL (N = 40 to 150 mg/dL), IgG is 60 mg/dL (N = 450 to 1,200 mg/dL), and IgA is undetectable (N = 20 to 100 mg/dL). B cell and T cell counts are normal. Genetic testing confirms X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his immunoglobulin pattern?
options: Absent CD40 on B cells and macrophages
Absent activation-induced cytidine deaminase in B cells
Absent CD40 ligand on activated CD4+ T cells
Absent Bruton tyrosine kinase in pre-B cells
approach: High IgM with low IgG, IgA, and IgE means B cells are present but cannot switch isotype.
Class switching needs CD40 ligand on activated helper T cells to bind CD40 on B cells.
X-linked inheritance and Pneumocystis infection point to the T cell side: the CD40 ligand gene (CD40LG) on the X chromosome.
questions.why: Isotype switching needs two signals from a helper T cell: CD40 ligand binding CD40 on the B cell, and cytokines such as IL-4 and IFN-gamma that choose the new isotype. Without CD40 ligand, B cells keep making IgM, and IgG, IgA, and IgE stay low. CD40 ligand also activates macrophages and dendritic cells through CD40, so cell-mediated immunity is weak. That is why these boys get Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium as well as pyogenic infections.
whyNot: CD40 deficiency gives a similar picture, but the CD40 gene is autosomal, so it would be autosomal recessive, not X-linked.
AID deficiency also blocks class switching, but it is autosomal recessive and leaves T cell help intact, so opportunistic infections are not typical.
Correct.
BTK deficiency causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia with absent B cells and low IgM.

questions.stem: CD40 ligand normally stimulates dendritic cells to increase their expression of B7 (CD80 and CD86). A naive CD4+ T cell recognizes a Pneumocystis peptide on MHC class II on a dendritic cell that expresses no B7. Which of the following outcomes is most likely for this T cell?
approach: Full activation of a naive T cell needs signal 1 (T cell receptor binding peptide on MHC) and signal 2 (CD28 binding B7).
Without B7 there is no costimulation through CD28.
Signal 1 alone makes the T cell unresponsive, which is anergy.
questions.why: Naive T cells need two signals. Signal 1 is the T cell receptor binding its peptide on MHC. Signal 2 is CD28 on the T cell binding B7 on the antigen-presenting cell. With signal 1 alone, the T cell becomes anergic and does not respond to later exposure. CD40 ligand normally boosts B7 and IL-12 on dendritic cells, which helps prime Th1 responses. Later, CTLA-4 and PD-1 on activated T cells send inhibitory signals that turn the response down.
whyNot: Clonal expansion needs both signal 1 and CD28 costimulation, which drive IL-2 production.
Memory cells form only after a full activation response with costimulation.
Th1 differentiation needs full activation plus IL-12 from the antigen-presenting cell.
Correct.

questions.stem: Dendritic cells carry Pneumocystis antigens from the lung to the hilar lymph nodes through afferent lymphatics. Naive T cells that recognize these antigens most likely entered the node through which of the following routes?
approach: Separate how antigen arrives (dendritic cells in afferent lymph) from how naive T cells arrive.
Naive lymphocytes circulate in blood and leave it in the node through specialized venules.
These high endothelial venules sit in the paracortex, the T cell zone.
questions.why: Naive lymphocytes move from blood to lymph node through high endothelial venules in the paracortex. L-selectin on the lymphocyte lets it roll on the venule wall, and the chemokine receptor CCR7 responds to chemokines made in the T cell zone, which triggers integrin binding and exit from the vessel. In the paracortex the T cells meet dendritic cells that brought antigen in through afferent lymph. Lymphocytes that are not activated leave through efferent lymph and return to the blood.
whyNot: Correct.
Afferent lymph brings dendritic cells and antigen into the node. Most naive T cells enter from the blood.
Efferent lymphatics are the exit route for lymphocytes leaving the node.
Medullary sinuses drain lymph toward the efferent vessel. They are not an entry route for naive T cells.

questions.stem: A biopsy of an enlarged cervical lymph node is performed. Which of the following abnormalities is most likely?
options: Absent B cells in the cortex
approach: Recall that germinal centers form inside cortical follicles when activated B cells receive T cell help.
That help depends on CD40 ligand binding CD40.
Without it, B cells fill primary follicles, but germinal centers do not form.
questions.why: The lymph node cortex holds B cell follicles. After antigen exposure, B cells that receive help from follicular helper T cells form germinal centers, where class switching, somatic hypermutation, and memory B cell formation take place. CD40 ligand is needed for germinal center formation. In X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome the follicles contain B cells but lack germinal centers, while the paracortex has normal numbers of T cells.
whyNot: His T cell numbers are normal, so the paracortex is populated. Paracortical depletion fits DiGeorge syndrome.
Correct.
His B cell numbers are normal, so the cortex has B cells. Absent cortical B cells fits X-linked agammaglobulinemia.
Sinus macrophage prominence (sinus histiocytosis) is a nonspecific reactive change, not the defining lesion of this disease.

case: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of ear pain and small red spots on his skin. He has had an itchy rash since age 2 months and two episodes of otitis media. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 90/58 mm Hg. Examination shows eczematous plaques on the cheeks and flexures, scattered petechiae, and a bulging right tympanic membrane. Platelet count is 32,000/mm3 (N = 150,000 to 450,000/mm3), and mean platelet volume is 5.6 fL (N = 7.5 to 11.5 fL). Serum IgM is 18 mg/dL (N = 40 to 150 mg/dL), IgA is 190 mg/dL (N = 15 to 90 mg/dL), IgE is 850 IU/mL (N less than 30 IU/mL), and IgG is normal. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the WAS gene. Diagnosis: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

questions.stem: His mother is found to be a heterozygous carrier of the mutation, and his father is unaffected. They plan another pregnancy, and the sex of the fetus is not yet known. Which of the following is the probability that their next child will be affected?
approach: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is X-linked recessive.
A carrier mother passes the mutant X to half her children, and only sons who receive it are affected.
Probability of a son (1/2) times probability he gets the mutant X (1/2) gives 1/4.
questions.why: The WAS gene is on the X chromosome, and the disease is X-linked recessive. Each child of a carrier mother has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting the mutant X. A son who inherits it is affected. A daughter who inherits it is usually an unaffected carrier, because she also receives a normal X from her father. With the sex unknown, the risk is 1/2 (son) times 1/2 (mutant X), or 25%. For a known son, the risk is 50%.
whyNot: Calculating 12.5% halves the risk one time too many. Only two independent events matter here: being male and inheriting the mutant X.
Correct.
50% is the risk for a son, not for a child of unknown sex.
75% is the chance that a child of two carrier parents gets at least one mutant allele in an autosomal recessive disease. It does not fit an X-linked disease with an unaffected father.

questions.stem: He also has poor antibody responses to polysaccharide antigens. In the spleen, which of the following cells normally produce the rapid IgM response that helps clear encapsulated bacteria from the blood?
approach: Capsular polysaccharides are T-independent antigens.
In the spleen, the B cells that answer T-independent antigens quickly with IgM sit in the marginal zone.
Their IgM, with marginal zone macrophages, clears encapsulated bacteria from blood.
questions.why: Blood flows through the splenic marginal zone, where macrophages and marginal zone B cells sample it. Marginal zone B cells respond rapidly to polysaccharide antigens and make IgM without much T cell help. IgM activates complement, and C3b-coated bacteria are removed by splenic macrophages. The spleen also removes aged red cells and inclusions and stores about a third of the platelets. Asplenia, or weak polysaccharide responses as in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, raises the risk of sepsis from encapsulated bacteria.
whyNot: Germinal center B cells give T-dependent, class-switched, high-affinity responses, which take days and need protein antigens.
The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath holds T cells, which cannot recognize polysaccharides and do not make antibody.
Red pulp macrophages remove aged red cells and opsonized particles but do not produce antibody.
Correct.

questions.stem: Within hours after bacteria enter his middle ear, and before any antibody is made, neutrophils and macrophages recognize the bacteria. The receptors these cells use for this recognition have which of the following properties?
approach: Hours after exposure, before antibody, points to innate immunity.
Innate cells use pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors.
These receptors are inherited unchanged in the germline and recognize molecules shared by many microbes.
questions.why: Innate immunity acts within minutes to hours. Its cells, such as neutrophils, macrophages, and NK cells, along with complement, use pattern recognition receptors coded in the germline. Every cell of a type carries the same receptors, which recognize conserved microbial molecules such as LPS or flagellin, and there is no memory. Adaptive immunity uses T and B cell receptors made by gene rearrangement. Each clone has its own specificity, responses take days, and repeat exposure brings faster, stronger responses through memory.
whyNot: Correct.
Somatic gene rearrangement creates T cell and B cell receptors, which belong to adaptive immunity.
Clonal distribution, with each cell carrying a unique receptor, is a feature of lymphocytes.
Rising affinity on repeat exposure comes from somatic hypermutation in B cells, an adaptive feature.

questions.stem: Many of his small platelets are destroyed in the spleen. In the open circulation of the red pulp, blood from arterial capillaries passes through which of the following before it enters the venous sinusoids?
approach: Trace splenic blood flow: trabecular artery, then central arteriole in the white pulp, then penicillar arterioles into the red pulp.
In the open circulation, blood empties into the cords of Billroth.
Cells must squeeze through slits in sinusoid walls to re-enter the circulation, and macrophages in the cords remove damaged cells and platelets.
questions.why: The white pulp is lymphoid tissue: the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath of T cells around central arterioles, B cell follicles, and the marginal zone. The red pulp has splenic cords and venous sinusoids. In the open circulation, blood leaves arterial capillaries into the cords of Billroth, then squeezes through narrow slits between sinusoid lining cells. Macrophages in the cords remove old or abnormal cells and antibody-coated platelets. Sinusoids drain to pulp veins, trabecular veins, and the splenic vein.
whyNot: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath surrounds the central arteriole in the white pulp, upstream of the red pulp.
Germinal centers lie in white pulp follicles and are not part of the red pulp blood path.
Correct.
Trabecular veins receive blood after it has passed through the sinusoids and pulp veins.

dx: Chronic granulomatous disease with Aspergillus pneumonia
case: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever and cough for 3 weeks. At age 3 years he had a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess, and he has had two episodes of suppurative cervical lymphadenitis that required drainage. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over the left upper lung. Leukocyte count is 14,800/mm3 (N = 4,500 to 13,500/mm3). CT of the chest shows multiple nodules. Lung biopsy shows granulomas and septate hyphae that branch at acute angles, and culture grows Aspergillus fumigatus. A dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test shows no increase in neutrophil fluorescence after stimulation. Diagnosis: X-linked chronic granulomatous disease with Aspergillus pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which of the following reactions is defective in this patient's neutrophils?
options: Hydrogen peroxide and chloride to hypochlorous acid
approach: The dihydrorhodamine test measures whether stimulated neutrophils make reactive oxygen species.
No change in fluorescence means the respiratory burst never starts.
The first enzyme of the burst is NADPH oxidase, which turns oxygen into superoxide using NADPH.
questions.why: The respiratory burst begins when NADPH oxidase in the phagosome membrane transfers electrons from NADPH to oxygen, making superoxide. Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase combines hydrogen peroxide with chloride to make hypochlorous acid (bleach). The pentose phosphate pathway supplies the NADPH. In chronic granulomatous disease, a defective NADPH oxidase subunit (most often the X-linked gp91phox) stops the burst at its first step, so the dihydrorhodamine test shows no oxidation.
whyNot: Correct.
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. It is downstream of the defect and has no substrate here.
Myeloperoxidase makes hypochlorous acid. Its deficiency leaves superoxide production intact and is usually mild, with Candida as the main risk.

G6PD makes NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway. Severe G6PD deficiency can weaken the burst, but it presents mainly with hemolysis. Chronic granulomatous disease is a defect of NADPH oxidase itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties of an organism best predicts that it will cause serious infection in this patient?
approach: His neutrophils cannot make their own hydrogen peroxide.
Many microbes make hydrogen peroxide as a by-product, which neutrophil myeloperoxidase can still use to kill them.
Catalase-positive organisms break down their own hydrogen peroxide, so the neutrophil has nothing to work with.
questions.why: CGD neutrophils can still use hydrogen peroxide made by the microbe inside the phagosome. Catalase destroys this hydrogen peroxide, so catalase-positive organisms survive. Typical CGD pathogens are catalase-positive: Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, and Nocardia. The diagnosis is made with an abnormal dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test or, in older practice, a nitroblue tetrazolium test that fails to turn blue.
whyNot: A polysaccharide capsule predicts infection in antibody, complement, or splenic defects, where opsonization fails.
Obligate intracellular organisms are controlled mainly by T cells and NK cells, which are normal in CGD.
Correct.
Lipooligosaccharide is the outer membrane endotoxin of Neisseria and Haemophilus. Recurrent Neisseria infection points to terminal complement deficiency, not to a phagocyte killing defect.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has partial albinism, peripheral neuropathy, recurrent pyogenic infections, and giant cytoplasmic granules in her neutrophils. Which of the following processes is most likely defective in her phagocytes?
approach: Giant granules, partial albinism, and neuropathy describe Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
Its LYST mutation disrupts lysosomal trafficking.
Lysosomes fuse into giant granules and fail to fuse with phagosomes, so ingested bacteria are not killed.
questions.why: Phagocytosis starts when IgG (binding Fc gamma receptors) and C3b (binding complement receptors) coat a microbe. The phagocyte engulfs it into a phagosome, which then fuses with lysosomes to form a phagolysosome. In Chediak-Higashi syndrome, an autosomal recessive LYST mutation impairs lysosomal trafficking. Giant granules form in neutrophils, melanosomes are not delivered normally (partial albinism), nerves are affected, and phagolysosome fusion fails, so pyogenic infections recur.
whyNot: NADPH oxidase is the defect in chronic granulomatous disease. Neutrophil granules and pigmentation are normal there.
Integrin-mediated adhesion fails in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, which brings delayed umbilical cord separation and infections without pus.
C3b generation fails in C3 deficiency, which causes pyogenic infections without giant granules or albinism.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two years earlier, a skin abscess on his thigh was drained and the wound was sutured. A firm nodule now present at the scar is excised. Microscopy shows macrophages, epithelioid cells, and multinucleated giant cells surrounding birefringent suture material, with few lymphocytes. Which of the following best distinguishes this lesion from an immune granuloma?
options: It lacks an antigen-specific Th1 response
It is built from activated epithelioid macrophages
approach: Birefringent suture material with giant cells and few lymphocytes describes a foreign body granuloma.
Ask what drives each granuloma type.
Foreign body granulomas form because macrophages cannot digest inert material. Immune granulomas need T cells that recognize antigen and release IFN-gamma.
questions.why: Both granuloma types are collections of activated macrophages, epithelioid cells, and often multinucleated giant cells. A foreign body granuloma forms around inert material too large to ingest, such as suture, talc, or a splinter. It needs no specific T cell response, and the material is often visible, sometimes birefringent under polarized light. An immune granuloma, as in tuberculosis or sarcoidosis, is driven by Th1 cells that recognize antigen and release IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages and draws a cuff of lymphocytes.
whyNot: Multinucleated giant cells appear in both immune and foreign body granulomas, so they do not tell them apart.
Correct.
Epithelioid macrophages make up both types of granuloma.
Caseous necrosis marks some immune granulomas, especially tuberculosis. It is not found in this lesion, and many immune granulomas lack it.

case: A 19-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of swelling of her lips and left hand and crampy abdominal pain with vomiting for 1 day. She has had similar episodes since age 12 years, often after dental work or minor injury. The swelling does not itch, and antihistamines have not helped. Her father has had similar episodes. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows nonpitting swelling of the lips and the back of the left hand without urticaria. There is no stridor. CT of the abdomen shows thickened, edematous loops of small bowel. Serum C1 esterase inhibitor concentration is 5 mg/dL (N = 21 to 39 mg/dL). Diagnosis: hereditary angioedema from C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following mediators is most directly responsible for her swelling?
approach: C1 esterase inhibitor controls C1 of the classical pathway and also kallikrein and factor XIIa of the contact system.
Without it, kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen and releases bradykinin.
Bradykinin raises vascular permeability without mast cell activation, so there is no itch or urticaria and antihistamines fail.
questions.why: C1 esterase inhibitor is a serine protease inhibitor. It inactivates C1r and C1s of the classical complement pathway and kallikrein and factor XIIa of the contact system. In hereditary angioedema, an autosomal dominant deficiency of this inhibitor lets kallikrein generate excess bradykinin, which increases venular permeability. Swelling of the skin, gut, and airway follows without hives or itch. Other complement regulators matter elsewhere: DAF (CD55) and CD59 protect red cells, and their loss in PIGA-mutant paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria causes intravascular hemolysis.
whyNot: Histamine from mast cells causes allergic angioedema with urticaria and itch, which respond to antihistamines.
C3a is an anaphylatoxin that can trigger mast cell release, but uncontrolled C1 mainly consumes C4 and C2 and does not explain bradykinin-type swelling without urticaria.
Platelet-activating factor is a mast cell and leukocyte lipid mediator in anaphylaxis, which brings urticaria and hypotension.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the accumulation of fluid in her tissues during an attack?
options: Filtration from leaky venules outpacing lymph flow
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from protein loss
Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure from venous block
Obstruction of lymphatic vessels draining the area
approach: Normally, Starling forces cause a small net filtration from capillaries, and lymphatics return it to the blood.
Bradykinin opens gaps between venular endothelial cells, so protein and fluid leak out much faster.
When filtration exceeds the maximum lymph flow, fluid collects in the interstitium.
questions.why: Fluid movement across capillaries depends on hydrostatic and oncotic pressures in the capillary and the interstitium. Normally, filtration slightly exceeds reabsorption, and lymphatics return the excess, about 2 to 3 L each day, to the blood. Bradykinin increases venular permeability, so protein leaks out. This lowers the oncotic gradient and raises filtration. When filtration outruns the lymphatics' capacity, edema forms, here in the lips, hand, and bowel wall.
whyNot: Correct.
Low plasma oncotic pressure, as in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis, causes generalized pitting edema that develops slowly, not episodic local swelling.
Raised hydrostatic pressure from venous obstruction, as in deep vein thrombosis, swells the drained limb but does not explain recurrent swelling in many sites.
Lymphatic obstruction, as after node dissection or in filariasis, causes persistent lymphedema, not attacks that resolve in days.

questions.stem: Serum complement studies are obtained during the attack. Which of the following patterns is most likely?
approach: Without C1 esterase inhibitor, activated C1s keeps cleaving its substrates, C4 and C2.
C4 is consumed, but C3 is not, because the activation does not proceed far down the cascade.
Low C4 with normal C3 is the typical screening pattern for hereditary angioedema.
questions.why: Complement levels point to where activation is happening. Unregulated C1 in hereditary angioedema cleaves C4 and C2, so C4 is low, while C3 stays normal. In active SLE, immune complexes drive the classical pathway all the way, so both C3 and C4 fall. In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, activation is mainly through the alternative pathway, so C3 is low and C4 is normal.
whyNot: Low C3 with normal C4 suggests alternative pathway activation, as in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Low C3 and C4 together suggest classical pathway consumption by immune complexes, as in active SLE.
Correct.
Normal C3 and C4 would be unusual in hereditary angioedema. C4 is low in most patients even between attacks.

questions.stem: Before diagnosis, her episodes were treated as allergic angioedema. In IgE-mediated angioedema, mast cells synthesize lipid mediators from arachidonic acid. Which of the following mediators both increases venular permeability and constricts bronchial smooth muscle?
approach: Split arachidonic acid products by enzyme: cyclooxygenase makes prostaglandins and thromboxane, and 5-lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes.
Among leukotrienes, LTB4 attracts neutrophils, while LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4 constrict airways and increase permeability.
So the mediator with both actions is LTD4.
questions.why: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids. Cyclooxygenase converts it to prostaglandins and thromboxane. PGE2 causes fever, pain, and vasodilation, and thromboxane A2 causes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. 5-Lipoxygenase makes LTB4, a strong neutrophil chemoattractant, and the cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4. These cysteinyl leukotrienes increase venular permeability and cause sustained bronchoconstriction in allergic reactions and asthma.
whyNot: LTB4 is a 5-lipoxygenase product whose main action is neutrophil chemotaxis and adhesion.
Correct.
PGE2 causes vasodilation, fever, and pain, and it relaxes rather than constricts airway smooth muscle.
Thromboxane A2 mainly aggregates platelets and constricts vessels. It does not increase venular permeability.

dx: Meningococcal sepsis with terminal complement (C7) deficiency
case: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after the onset of fever, headache, and a spreading rash. He had meningococcal meningitis at age 12 years. Temperature is 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 78/40 mm Hg. He is lethargic and has neck stiffness. There are nonblanching purpuric lesions on the legs and trunk. Leukocyte count is 22,000/mm3 (N = 4,500 to 11,000/mm3), and platelet count is 60,000/mm3 (N = 150,000 to 450,000/mm3). Prothrombin time is prolonged. Blood cultures grow gram-negative diplococci identified as Neisseria meningitidis. After recovery, total hemolytic complement (CH50) is undetectable, C3 and C4 are normal, and C7 is absent. Diagnosis: meningococcal sepsis with terminal complement (C7) deficiency.

questions.stem: Another patient, a 7-year-old girl, has had recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia and bacteremia since infancy, and a kidney biopsy shows immune complex glomerulonephritis. Total hemolytic complement (CH50) and alternative pathway hemolytic activity (AH50) are both undetectable. Deficiency of which of the following complement proteins most likely explains her findings?
approach: CH50 and AH50 both absent means the missing protein is shared by the classical and alternative pathways: C3 or a terminal component (C5 to C9).
Severe pyogenic infections mean opsonization is failing, which a terminal component defect would not cause.
C3 is needed for both C3b opsonization and immune complex clearance, so its deficiency explains both findings.
questions.why: Each complement deficiency has a typical pattern. C3 deficiency removes the main opsonin and the central step of all three pathways, giving severe infections with encapsulated bacteria and immune complex glomerulonephritis. Deficiency of C1q, C2, or C4 mainly causes SLE-like immune complex disease. Deficiency of C5 to C9 causes recurrent Neisseria infections, as in the boy in this case. Mannose-binding lectin deficiency increases infections in early childhood.
whyNot: C1q deficiency mainly causes SLE-like disease. It blocks only the classical pathway, so AH50 would be normal, and C3b can still form through the alternative and lectin pathways.
C7 deficiency also makes CH50 and AH50 undetectable, but C3b opsonization is intact, so it causes recurrent Neisseria infection rather than pneumococcal disease and glomerulonephritis.
Correct.
C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema with low C4. It does not abolish CH50 and AH50 or cause pyogenic infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following complement functions is absent in this patient?
approach: C7 is part of the terminal pathway, after C5 is cleaved.
C5a and C3b are made before C7 acts, so they are still available.
The step lost is assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), which lyses Neisseria.
questions.why: Complement has several effector functions. C3b coats microbes for phagocytosis and helps clear immune complexes. C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that trigger mast cell release, and C5a also draws neutrophils. C5b binds C6, C7, C8, and many C9 molecules to form the membrane attack complex, a pore that lyses cells. Neisseria are especially vulnerable to this lysis. In C7 deficiency, cleavage up through C5 is intact, but the pore never forms, so Neisseria infections recur.
whyNot: C3b is made upstream of C7, so opsonization still works. That is why he is not prone to all encapsulated bacteria.
Correct.
C5a is released when C5 is cleaved, before C7 is needed, so neutrophil chemotaxis is preserved.
C3a is produced early in the cascade and is unaffected by loss of C7.

questions.stem: Which of the following interactions most directly starts the cytokine release responsible for his hypotension and purpura?
approach: He meets SIRS criteria: temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F), pulse above 90/min, respirations above 20/min, and leukocytes above 12,000/mm3.
The organism is gram-negative, and its endotoxin in Neisseria is lipooligosaccharide.
Endotoxin binds TLR4 (with CD14 and MD-2) on macrophages, which release TNF, IL-1, and IL-6.
questions.why: Endotoxin is the lipid A-containing glycolipid of the gram-negative outer membrane. In Neisseria it takes the form of lipooligosaccharide. With CD14 and MD-2, it binds TLR4 on monocytes and macrophages. NF-kB signaling then drives release of TNF, IL-1, and IL-6. These cytokines cause fever, vasodilation, capillary leak, and tissue factor expression, leading to hypotension, DIC with purpura, and organ dysfunction. SIRS criteria include temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F) or below 36 °C (96.8 °F), pulse above 90/min, respirations above 20/min, and leukocytes above 12,000/mm3 or below 4,000/mm3.
whyNot: Correct.
Peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid signal through TLR2 and are the main triggers in gram-positive sepsis.
Flagellin activates TLR5, but Neisseria are not flagellated.
Unmethylated CpG DNA activates TLR9 inside endosomes. It is not the main driver of gram-negative septic shock.

questions.stem: TNF and IL-1 released during his infection increase expression of ICAM-1 on endothelial cells. Neutrophils bind ICAM-1 for firm adhesion through which of the following molecules?
approach: Order the steps of extravasation: rolling, firm adhesion, diapedesis, then chemotaxis.
Rolling uses selectins and sialyl Lewis X. Firm adhesion uses neutrophil beta-2 integrins binding endothelial ICAM-1.
The beta-2 integrin LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18) binds ICAM-1.
questions.why: Neutrophils leave blood in a fixed order. They first roll along the endothelium as E-selectin and P-selectin bind sialyl Lewis X. TNF and IL-1 increase endothelial ICAM-1, and chemokines such as IL-8 activate neutrophil beta-2 integrins (LFA-1 and Mac-1, which share CD18). These integrins bind ICAM-1 and stop the cell. PECAM-1 then guides diapedesis between endothelial cells, and the neutrophil follows C5a, LTB4, and IL-8 to the infection. CD18 deficiency causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency.
whyNot: L-selectin on leukocytes helps with rolling and lymphocyte homing, not firm adhesion to ICAM-1.
PECAM-1 (CD31) works in diapedesis, the step after firm adhesion.
Sialyl Lewis X is the ligand that binds endothelial selectins during rolling.
Correct.
